analysis.one_liner: Repeals major parts of the Affordable Care Act and cuts its taxes on high earners and health industries.
analysis.headline: The bill passed both chambers along party lines, but President Obama vetoed it on January 8, 2016, and a House override vote on February 2 fell short at 241-186, needing a two-thirds majority.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repealed the heart of the Affordable Care Act: premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies for people buying coverage on their own, the Medicaid expansion, the individual and employer penalty for not carrying coverage, and a long list of ACA taxes. It also blocked federal Medicaid funds from going to Planned Parenthood for one year, ended the ACA's Prevention and Public Health Fund, and added two years of grants to states for substance abuse and mental health. Its tax repeals included the tax on investment income for high earners and the extra Medicare tax on high incomes, plus industry fees on insurers, drug makers, and medical device makers [S5] [S6].
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most in cash: the bill repealed the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% additional Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above the high-income thresholds [S5] [S6]. Health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and medical device makers gain because the ACA's annual fees on them are repealed [S5]. Some middle-class households gain smaller amounts through ending the individual mandate penalty, letting health savings accounts pay for over-the-counter drugs, and removing limits on flexible spending accounts [S5]. Community health centers gain increased funding, and states receive two years of grants for substance abuse and mental health programs [S5] [S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax on high incomes, directly cutting taxes for the highest-earning households [S5] [S6].
Eliminates the individual mandate penalty and large-employer penalty, so people who did not buy coverage no longer owe a tax penalty [S5] [S6].

Allows HSAs, medical savings accounts, and flexible spending accounts to pay for over-the-counter medications, lowers the penalty on non-medical HSA withdrawals, and removes the annual cap on flexible spending contributions [S5] [S6].
Repeals ACA fees on health insurers, brand-name prescription drug manufacturers and importers, and medical device sales [S5] [S6].
Increases community health center funding and appropriates $750 million per year for fiscal 2016 and 2017 for state substance abuse and urgent mental health programs [S5] [S6].
Repeals the excise tax on high-cost employer health plans (the 'Cadillac tax') after 2017 [S5] [S6].

analysis.who_pays: The largest costs fall on people who buy coverage on their own and on low-income adults: the bill ends the premium tax credit, cost-sharing subsidies, and Medicaid expansion after December 31, 2017 [S5] [S6]. It requires people to pay back the full amount of any excess advance premium credit with no cap [S5]. Patients of family planning providers lose: for one year no federal Medicaid funds may go to Planned Parenthood or any similar entity [S5] [S6]. The Prevention and Public Health Fund, which paid for prevention programs, is terminated and unobligated funds are rescinded [S5] [S6]. The $379 billion transfer the bill directs to the Medicare trust fund is paid for by those repeals and cuts, so the lost health coverage and funding are the price [S6].
analysis.who_pays_short: People with subsidized coverage and Medicaid expansion

drawbacks.text: Ends premium tax credits, cost-sharing subsidies, and the Medicaid expansion after December 31, 2017, removing the subsidies that made coverage affordable for millions of lower- and middle-income people [S5] [S6].
Repeals the tax on high earners' investment income and wages, which was one of the ACA's main funding sources, and replaces the lost revenue with coverage cuts [S5] [S6].
Cuts off federal Medicaid payments to Planned Parenthood and similar providers for one year, based on a definition that covers a single large provider [S5] [S6].
Terminates the Prevention and Public Health Fund and rescinds its unobligated money, eliminating ACA funding for prevention programs [S5] [S6].
The substance abuse and mental health grants are appropriated for only fiscal 2016 and 2017, so that new help expires alongside the coverage repeal [S6].

Ends Medicaid presumptive-eligibility elections and minimum essential benefit requirements in Medicaid benchmark plans after 2017, reducing what Medicaid covers and how easily people can enroll [S5] [S6].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real but skewed: the biggest cash benefits go to the highest earners through repeal of the net investment income and additional Medicare taxes, and to insurers, drug makers, and device makers through fee repeal. The largest cost falls on people who rely on ACA subsidies and the Medicaid expansion, which end completely after 2017. The two-year substance abuse grants and health center funding are genuine public benefits, but they are temporary and small next to the coverage and tax provisions. On balance, the bill trades broad coverage subsidies and provider funding for tax cuts concentrated at the top and on health industry fees.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed it, President Obama vetoed it, and the House's override vote got 241 votes when it needed two-thirds, so it never became law.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on October 23, 2015, 240-189, with Republicans voting 239-7 in favor and Democrats voting 1-182 against [S9].
The Senate amended the bill and passed it 52-47 on December 3, 2015, with all 52 Republicans voting yes and no Democrats or independents voting yes [S10] [S8].
The House agreed to the Senate amendment on January 6, 2016, 240-181, again almost entirely on party lines [S11] [S8].
The bill was presented to the President on January 7, 2016, and vetoed on January 8, 2016 [S8].

On February 2, 2016, the House voted to override the veto but failed 241-186, short of the two-thirds majority required, with 240 of 245 voting Republicans in favor and only 1 of 188 voting Democrats [S12] [S8].
Because the veto stood, the bill never became law, and the ACA subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and taxes it targeted remained in effect.

This was the first time Congress passed a full ACA repeal through the budget reconciliation process and sent it to a president's desk; the same party majority that passed it used the same route to try again in 2017.

Supporters designed it through reconciliation, a process that allows budget-related provisions to pass the Senate with a simple majority and avoid a 60-vote filibuster; the bill was reported by the House Budget Committee as an original measure pursuant to the FY2016 budget resolution [S1] [S3].
Sponsor Tom Price later became HHS Secretary, and the substance abuse grant section of this bill became the model for the 21st Century Cures Act's state opioid grants in 2016.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low- and middle-income people who depend on ACA premium subsidies, cost-sharing help, and the Medicaid expansion came out ahead, because the veto preserved their coverage and the high-income tax cuts and industry fee repeals never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People on ACA subsidies and Medicaid

for.name: Tom Price
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-GA), sponsor; chairman, House Budget Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, reported it from the Budget Committee as an original measure, and managed it on the House floor, including the motion to accept the Senate amendment [S1] [S8].

for.name: House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted overwhelmingly to pass the bill (239-7) on October 23, 2015, to accept the Senate amendment (239-3) on January 6, 2016, and to override the veto (240-3) on February 2, 2016 [S9] [S11] [S12].

for.name: 52 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill 52-47 with an amendment on December 3, 2015, over unanimous Democratic opposition [S10].

for.name: House Republican leadership
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a rule limiting debate, and when the veto came back, Republicans initially delayed the override vote twice before scheduling it for February 2, 2016 [S8].

for.name: Senate Democratic and independent leadership
for.role: Minority Leader Harry Reid and Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted unanimously against the bill and against the motion to proceed; their stated objection was the Planned Parenthood defunding rider and the repeal of coverage subsidies [S10].

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on January 8, 2016, calling it a repeal of provisions that help millions of Americans get affordable coverage, and his veto was sustained when the override vote fell short [S8].

against.name: 186 House members voting to sustain the veto
against.role: Coalition of House Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 independent
against.what_they_did: Voted against overriding the veto on February 2, 2016, holding the override below the two-thirds threshold (241-186) [S12].

against.name: 44 of 44 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
against.role: Senate Democratic caucus and allied independents
against.what_they_did: Voted unanimously against passage on December 3, 2015 (52-47) [S10].

against.name: 2 Senate Republicans
against.role: Republican senators voting no on passage
against.what_they_did: Joined Democrats in voting no on final Senate passage [S10].

sides.party_line_note: The vote split almost perfectly by party: the House passed it 240-189 with 239 of 246 voting Republicans in favor and 1 of 188 voting Democrats; the Senate passed it 52-47 with all 52 voting Republicans in favor and no Democrats or independents; and the failed override was 241-186 with 240 of 245 voting Republicans for it [S9] [S10] [S12].

industries.note: The bill repeals the ACA's annual fee on health insurers, cutting their costs, but also repeals the premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies that made millions of people paying customers, and eliminates the individual mandate that kept younger, healthier people in the market [S5] [S6].

The annual fee on brand-name drug manufacturers and importers is repealed, removing roughly $2-3 billion a year in industry costs; the revenue that paid for it is not replaced, and consumers see no direct benefit [S5] [S6].
The 2.3% excise tax on medical device sales is repealed entirely, a direct tax cut to the industry, funded by the broader repeal that also cuts coverage subsidies [S5] [S6].

Repeal of the net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax gives the largest per-dollar benefit to households with high investment and wage income, and is paid for by ending subsidies and coverage that mostly help lower incomes [S5] [S6].

The bill increases Medicaid disproportionate share hospital allotments, offsetting some of the loss from ending the Medicaid expansion, and ends hospital presumptive eligibility elections after 2017, reducing uncompensated-care screening [S5] [S6].

industries.industry: Planned Parenthood and family planning providers
industries.note: For one year, no federal Medicaid funds may go to Planned Parenthood or any similar provider, which reduces access to contraception, cancer screenings, and other services for people who rely on them [S5] [S6].
Funding for community health centers is increased, which expands access to primary care for low-income patients [S5] [S6].
The ACA's 10% indoor tanning services tax is repealed, a small industry-specific tax cut [S5] [S6].
